html:
The Tao Te Ching, "the Classic of the Way and its Virtue", is a short Chinese book of poetic sayings, traditionally said to be by the sage Laozi. It is the founding text of Taoism and one of the most translated books in the world.

It has about five thousand characters in 81 short chapters. Its dating and authorship are debated. Most scholars think sayings linked to Laozi were written down from the late 5th century BCE and gathered into versions during the 4th century BCE, in the Warring States period. The oldest manuscript pieces, the Guodian bamboo slips, date from around 300 BCE. Fuller silk copies were found at Mawangdui in a tomb of 168 BCE.

Its central ideas:

  • The Tao, the Way, is the source of all things. It cannot be fully named or described.
  • Wu wei, acting without forcing, is the wise way to live and to rule.
  • Water is the model: soft and yielding, yet it wears away stone.
  • The best ruler governs so lightly that the people hardly know he is there.

It reads in part as advice to rulers, and in part as a mystical poem. It pushed back against the Confucian stress on ritual and effort. Later thinkers of every school, Legalists, Confucians and above all Chinese Buddhists, read it and borrowed its words.

Together with the Zhuangzi, it gave Chinese culture a lasting second voice beside Confucius: one of nature, spontaneity and withdrawal from the struggle for power.
sum: The Tao Te Ching, "the Classic of the Way and its Virtue", is a short Chinese book of poetic sayings, traditionally said to be by the sage Laozi. It is the founding text of Taoism and one of the most translated books in the world.
